lesson.title: The Knife Edge Between Ringing and Sluggish: Critical Damping
lesson.summary: Critical damping is the exact boundary where the two real roots of an overdamped circuit merge into one repeated root, giving the fastest possible return to equilibrium with no overshoot at all.
lesson.body:
Critical damping is the precise dividing line between the overdamped and underdamped cases, occurring when alpha equals omega0 exactly, so zeta = alpha/omega0 = 1. At that exact point the discriminant alpha^2 - omega0^2 in the characteristic equation is zero, and the two roots that were spreading apart in the overdamped case or splitting into a complex pair in the underdamped case instead collide into a single repeated real root, s = -alpha. A repeated root changes the form of the general solution: it is no longer A1 e^(s1 t) + A2 e^(s2 t), because with s1 = s2 that would just be one constant times one exponential, not enough freedom to satisfy two independent initial conditions. Instead the second solution picks up an extra factor of t, giving x(t) = (A1 + A2 t) e^(-alpha t).

Critical damping matters in practice because it gives the fastest possible decay to zero with no overshoot whatsoever, a combination overdamped circuits cannot match, since their dominant slow root always drags the response out longer, and underdamped circuits cannot match either, since they overshoot and ring before settling. That is why galvanometer needles, some shock absorbers, and many control system designs are tuned deliberately to sit as close to zeta = 1 as manufacturing tolerances allow: it is the sweet spot between too slow and too jumpy.

Return once more to the R, L, C family from this chapter's earlier examples, now with R raised to 32 ohms, L = 4 H, C = 1/64 F. As before omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC) = 4 rad/s, and the damping coefficient is alpha = R/(2L) = 32/(2 times 4) = 32/8 = 4 rad/s. Since alpha = omega0 = 4 exactly, this circuit sits precisely at critical damping, zeta = 1. The characteristic equation is s^2 + 8s + 16 = 0, which factors as (s + 4)^2 = 0, confirming the single repeated root s = -4 rad/s directly, without even needing the quadratic formula.

Suppose this circuit's current starts at i(0) = 2 A with initial slope i'(0) = -2 A/s. The general solution is i(t) = (A1 + A2 t) e^(-4t). Setting t = 0 gives i(0) = A1 = 2. Differentiating, i'(t) = A2 e^(-4t) - 4(A1 + A2 t) e^(-4t), and at t = 0 this is A2 - 4A1 = -2, so A2 = -2 + 4(2) = 6. The full response is i(t) = (2 + 6t) e^(-4t) amperes. Checking: i(0) = (2 + 0)(1) = 2, correct, and i'(t) = 6e^(-4t) - 4(2 + 6t)e^(-4t) = (-2 - 24t)e^(-4t), which at t = 0 gives -2, matching the assumed initial slope exactly.

Notice that this circuit used the same L and C as the overdamped and underdamped examples in the last two chapters, only R changed, from 40 ohms down to 8 ohms and now to 32 ohms, squarely in between in the sense that matters, the one where alpha meets omega0. That progression is the clearest way to see what damping ratio actually measures: it is not really about R, L, or C individually, it is about the balance between how fast the resistor drains energy and how fast the inductor and capacitor would oscillate on their own.
